cards.title: The Incident Commander
cards.teaser: The Incident Commander is the single decision-maker during an incident — not the best debugger in the room, but the person who keeps the room pointed at the right problem, makes calls when the team is stuck, and delegates relentlessly. IC and Ops Lead are different jobs.

runs.text: The Incident Commander (IC) role originates in emergency management — the Incident Command System (ICS) developed by US firefighters in the 1970s to coordinate multi-agency disaster response. Google's Site Reliability Engineering book and PagerDuty's Incident Response Process (IRP) both adapted it for software operations, and the pattern has become the industry standard.
The IC's responsibilities during an incident:

items.text: Hold authority.
The IC makes binding decisions. When two engineers disagree on a mitigation path, the IC chooses one and moves on. Consensus is a luxury; incidents run on authority.
Maintain situational awareness.
The IC tracks what every sub-team is doing, what has been tried, and what the current best theory of the failure is. They are the single coherent model of the incident.
Delegate, not debug.
The IC does not touch the keyboard. The moment an IC starts debugging, they stop commanding — situational awareness degrades, decisions get delayed, and the war room loses its coordinator.
Manage cognitive load.
The IC runs the meeting cadence, limits who is speaking at any time, and surfaces blockers before they stall the investigation.
Declare severity and escalate.
The IC makes the formal severity call and decides when to pull in additional resources, leadership, or vendors.

runs.text: The hardest part of the IC role for engineers is restraint. Senior engineers are conditioned to solve problems personally. During an incident, the IC's job is to
enable others to solve the problem
— which means staying out of the terminal and staying in the meta-view.

An IC who starts debugging has effectively vacated the IC role. Either hand the IC hat to someone else before you start investigating, or stay in the IC role and keep your hands off the keyboard. Doing both simultaneously is how incidents spiral.

The Incident Commander is the person who runs the incident without personally debugging it. They keep everyone pointed at the right problem, make decisions when the team is stuck, and hand off authority cleanly when their shift ends.

cards.title: IC vs Operations Lead: Role Boundaries
cards.teaser: IC and Ops Lead are often confused because both are senior engineers — but they are doing entirely different jobs. The IC owns the process; the Ops Lead owns the technical investigation. Mixing them collapses the incident structure.

runs.text: In Google's Incident Management Process (IMP) and in PagerDuty's IRP, three roles are defined as the core incident team for any significant incident: the Incident Commander, the Operations Lead, and the Communications Lead. Understanding the precise boundary between IC and Ops Lead is essential because they are both typically senior engineers and the boundary is easy to blur under pressure.

items.text: Incident Commander
— owns the incident process: cadence, escalation, severity, communications coordination, and ultimately the declaration and close. Does not write code or run commands.
Operations Lead

— owns the technical investigation: hypothesizing failure modes, directing engineers to gather specific data, evaluating mitigation options, and executing or approving changes. The Ops Lead is in the terminal. The IC is not.

runs.text: The Ops Lead reports to the IC on investigation status at a regular cadence (every 10-15 minutes in a SEV-1). The IC does not tell the Ops Lead how to investigate — they ask for status and escalate blockers. The Ops Lead does not manage the external communications or run the status page — that belongs to the Communications Lead.
Comparison at a glance:

items.text: IC asks: "What is the current status? What is the next action? What is blocking us?" Ops Lead answers.
IC decides: "We escalate to the database vendor." Ops Lead executes or assigns the escalation.
Ops Lead decides: "We need to run a live query against the replica." IC does not override technical decisions unless they conflict with incident policy.
IC closes the incident. Ops Lead confirms no outstanding technical risks before close.

runs.text: For small teams or smaller incidents, one senior engineer may wear both hats. This is a concession to reality, not best practice. As soon as a second senior engineer joins, split the roles explicitly.

The IC runs the meeting; the Ops Lead runs the investigation. The IC does not touch the terminal; the Ops Lead does. When both roles collapse into one person, you have no one watching the clock and no one managing the room.

cards.title: Communications Lead
cards.teaser: The Communications Lead is the bridge between the incident room and every audience that is not in the incident room: customers, support, executives, and the status page. Their job is to translate technical reality into appropriate language for each audience — without creating confusion or false hope.

runs.text: During a significant incident, engineers need to focus entirely on mitigation. The Communications Lead removes the context-switching cost of managing external inquiries. Without a dedicated Comms Lead, the IC or Ops Lead ends up writing status page updates between debugging sessions — which degrades both the investigation and the communications.
Communications Lead responsibilities:

items.text: Status page updates.

Own the public status page. Post an initial acknowledgment within 5 minutes of a SEV-1 declaration. Update at regular intervals (every 15-30 minutes) even when there is no new information — "We are investigating and have no update yet" is a valid update.
Internal updates.
Push regular summaries to internal Slack channels, support teams, and leadership. Internal communications can include more technical detail than public communications, but must still be accurate.
Support liaison.
Give the support team a holding response for affected customers. Ensure support does not promise timelines the engineering team has not committed to.
Executive escalation.
For SEV-1s, notify executives according to the escalation policy. The Comms Lead owns this; the IC should not be simultaneously briefing the CEO and managing the war room.

runs.text: Internal vs external content differs significantly. Internal: "We believe the root cause is a memory leak in the v2.14.3 deployment; we are testing a rollback." External: "We are experiencing elevated error rates on API requests and are actively investigating." External communications should never speculate on root cause, never promise resolution timelines, and never assign blame.
The Comms Lead must never invent information. If the status is unknown, the status update says "unknown." Guessing publicly and being wrong compounds the incident with a trust crisis.

The Communications Lead is the incident's spokesperson to the outside world. They translate the engineering team's current understanding into appropriate language for customers, support, and executives — and they post updates regularly even when there is nothing new to say.

cards.title: The Scribe Role
cards.teaser: The scribe builds the incident timeline in real time — who said what, what was tried, when things changed. Without a scribe, the post-incident review reconstructs events from memory, which is unreliable within hours. The timeline is evidence, not minutes.

runs.text: The scribe is the least glamorous role and the most undervalued. Their output — the incident timeline document — is the raw material for the post-mortem, the root cause analysis, and every improvement action that follows. Without a real-time scribe, the team is working from memory in the post-mortem, and memory degrades fast.
What the scribe records:

items.text: Timestamped events.
Every significant observation, decision, and action with an exact timestamp. "14:23 UTC — Ops Lead noticed elevated 5xx rate on /checkout endpoint. First alert fired at 14:21." Not prose; a log.
Hypotheses and their outcomes.
"14:31 — Hypothesis: connection pool exhaustion. Checked DB metrics. Ruled out at 14:35."
Commands and changes.
Every configuration change, rollback, restart, or manual intervention with the name of the person who made it and the outcome.
IC and Comms decisions.
Severity declarations, escalation calls, status page updates, and their timestamps.
Handoff notes.
A snapshot of current status, open hypotheses, and next actions at every shift handoff.

runs.text: The scribe is not an editor — do not clean up the timeline during the incident. Record everything as it happens; clean up afterward. Messy real-time notes are more valuable than polished retrospective prose.

PagerDuty's IRP recommends a shared document (Google Doc, Notion, Confluence) that all responders can see in real time. The scribe owns the document but anyone can add observations. The IC should be able to glance at the timeline to orient themselves at any moment.

The scribe writes down everything that happens during the incident — every decision, every command, every observation, with timestamps. This document is what makes the post-mortem accurate instead of a collective exercise in reconstructing foggy memories.

cards.title: Declaring an Incident
cards.teaser: The hardest part of declaring an incident is overcoming the instinct to wait until you are sure it is serious enough. The correct bias is to declare early and downgrade later. An undeclared incident that turns out to be serious is far more costly than a declared incident that resolves in 20 minutes.

runs.text: An incident is declared when something affecting users or system health requires coordinated response beyond what the on-call engineer can handle alone. The trigger is not certainty about severity — it is the need for coordination.
Common declaration triggers:

items.text: An SLO error budget is burning at an elevated rate and the cause is unknown.
A critical user journey (checkout, login, payment) is degraded or unavailable.
An alert has fired and investigation shows user-visible impact.
A deployment is behaving unexpectedly and rollback is being considered.
Multiple on-call engineers are already working the same problem in parallel without coordination.

runs.text: The act of declaring does three things: it activates the incident response structure (IC, Ops Lead, Comms Lead, Scribe), it starts the timeline, and it makes the event legible to the organization. Even a 20-minute incident that resolves quickly produces a timeline entry, which feeds the trend data that prevents the next one.
A key heuristic from PagerDuty's IRP:
lower the bar to declare

. The cost of a false declaration is a few engineers spending 20 minutes before standing down. The cost of a late declaration is uncoordinated response, late communications, and a post-mortem that cannot explain why the response was slow.

Many teams track "incidents declared" as a positive metric, not a negative one. High declaration rates mean the team has a low barrier to coordination, which typically means faster time to mitigation. Incident drought often means incidents are going undeclared.

Declare an incident when you need more than one person coordinating on a problem. Declare early and downgrade later if it turns out to be minor. The cost of a false alarm is low; the cost of coordinating too late is high.

cards.title: Incident Severity Levels
cards.teaser: Severity levels are the shared language that determines who gets paged, how fast communications go out, and how much organizational attention the incident warrants. A severity matrix that nobody can remember in the moment is not a severity matrix — it is documentation theater.

runs.text: Most organizations define three to five severity levels. The specifics vary, but the pattern is consistent: SEV-1 is the worst, SEV-5 (or the highest number) is the mildest. The level determines escalation, response SLAs, and communications requirements.
A typical severity matrix:

items.text: SEV-1 (Critical).

Complete outage of a critical service, or major data loss/corruption risk. All hands. IC activated. Executive escalation. Status page update within 5 minutes. Example: payment service returning 500 for all requests.
SEV-2 (Major).

Significant degradation affecting a large percentage of users, or a critical feature unavailable. IC activated. Status page updated. On-call team plus relevant owners. Example: checkout latency 10x normal, 30% of requests timing out.
SEV-3 (Moderate).
Partial degradation of a non-critical feature, or a workaround exists. No IC required. Scoped to on-call team. Internal notice only. Example: image upload failing for 5% of users.
SEV-4 / SEV-5 (Minor).
Cosmetic issues, single-user reports, or failures with no user impact. Tracked in the issue tracker, handled during business hours.

runs.text: Severity can be upgraded or downgraded as the incident evolves. An incident declared as SEV-2 that turns out to affect all paid users should be upgraded to SEV-1 immediately — the severity level should reflect the current reality, not the initial assessment. Upgrading severity is a decision the IC makes; it does not require consensus.

The most common severity error is under-declaring: calling a SEV-1 a SEV-2 to avoid the higher escalation overhead. This delays executive awareness and customer communications during the incidents where speed matters most. When in doubt, start at the higher severity and downgrade.

Severity levels are a shared language for how bad an incident is — they determine who gets woken up, how fast communications go out, and how much of the organization needs to be involved. They should be declared early, based on user impact, and upgraded immediately if the situation turns out to be worse than assessed.

cards.title: The War Room
cards.teaser: The war room is the single coordination channel for an incident — one Slack room or one bridge call, not several. Fragmented coordination across multiple channels is one of the most reliable ways to extend incident duration.

runs.text: The war room is the canonical place where the incident happens. All communication, investigation updates, decisions, and commands flow through it. The goal is to make the incident state legible to anyone who joins — a responder arriving 30 minutes in should be able to read the channel or call backlog and understand the current situation.
War room hygiene rules:

items.text: One channel per incident.
Create a dedicated Slack channel (e.g.,
#inc-2024-01-15-checkout
) at declaration time. Do not run the incident in an existing team channel — context gets lost in other traffic.
Minimize noise.
The war room is not a brainstorm channel. IC controls the agenda. Off-topic hypotheses, status inquiries from uninvolved parties, and general chatter are redirected out.
Keep a running status line.
The IC or scribe pins a short summary to the channel: current severity, current best hypothesis, what is being tried, and ETA for next update. This reduces the "what's happening" interruptions.
No side channels for decisions.
If two engineers make a decision in a DM or a side call that affects the incident, it must be posted back to the war room immediately. Decisions made outside the war room vanish from the timeline.
Manage observers.

Leadership and curious engineers watching the incident channel should be reminded to mute notifications on the channel and only read. "Helpful" commentary from non-responders is a cognitive load tax on the people doing the work.

runs.text: Some organizations use an actual physical war room (a conference room). The same hygiene rules apply: one conversation at a time, IC controls who speaks, side conversations happen outside the room. Physical war rooms work well for colocated teams on extended SEV-1s where coordination is complex enough to benefit from in-person presence.

The war room is the one channel where the incident lives — one Slack room or one call, not five. Everything flows through it, and it is kept clean enough that anyone joining mid-incident can catch up by reading backward.

cards.title: The Incident Bridge
cards.teaser: The incident bridge is the synchronous call that activates during a SEV-1 or SEV-2 — where the IC runs the meeting, engineering investigates live, and the Comms Lead takes notes for the next status update. It supplements the war room; it does not replace it.

runs.text: The incident bridge is a live voice or video call that runs concurrently with the war room chat channel. Chat is asynchronous and creates a written record; the bridge is synchronous and enables faster coordination when typed communication becomes a bottleneck.
When to open the bridge:

items.text: Automatically for SEV-1 declarations in most organizations. The bridge link is in the incident template.
When the war room chat is producing too much latency — when a question and answer cycle takes 3 minutes in chat, a bridge collapses it to 30 seconds.
When multiple people need to coordinate on a live change — a rollback, a schema migration, a load balancer reconfiguration — simultaneously.

runs.text: Bridge discipline matters as much as war room discipline:

items.text: IC facilitates.
The IC runs the meeting agenda: status check-ins from Ops Lead, next actions, blockers. One person speaks at a time.
Key decisions go back to chat.
Anything decided on the bridge is typed back into the war room channel immediately. The bridge is ephemeral; the chat channel is the record.
Drop observers.
Anyone on the bridge who is not actively contributing to investigation or decision-making should mute or drop. Large bridge calls create cognitive overhead.

runs.text: Google's IMP notes that bridge calls work best when the IC gives explicit airtime: "Ops Lead, status?" rather than opening the floor. Open floors in high-stress incidents devolve into crosstalk within minutes.

The incident bridge is a live call that runs alongside the war room channel. It speeds up coordination when chat becomes too slow. The IC runs it like a tight meeting: one person at a time, and key decisions get typed back into the channel so the record stays complete.

cards.title: The Status Page
cards.teaser: The status page is the public contract with customers during an incident. Tools like Atlassian Statuspage and Instatus make it easy to post updates — but the policy of what to say, when to say it, and how to phrase it matters more than the tool.

runs.text: The status page serves two purposes simultaneously: it informs affected customers of the current situation, and it reduces the volume of support contacts during an outage. A well-maintained status page is also a trust signal — it demonstrates operational transparency even when things are broken.
Common tools:

items.text: Atlassian Statuspage
— the most widely used hosted status page. Supports components, metric displays, subscriber emails, and RSS. Integrates with PagerDuty for automatic incident creation.
Instatus
— a lighter alternative with a generous free tier. Popular with smaller engineering teams.
Self-hosted options
— some organizations run their own (Cachet, Gatus). The advantage is that the status page does not depend on the outaged vendor's infrastructure.

runs.text: Status page communication policy:

items.text: Post within 5 minutes of a SEV-1 declaration.
Even if the update is only: "We are investigating an issue affecting [service]. Updates to follow."
Update on a regular cadence
— every 15-30 minutes. A status page that goes dark for an hour signals worse management than the incident itself.
Never speculate publicly.
"Root cause appears to be a database migration" is speculation. "We are investigating" is not. Save the root cause for the post-mortem.
Post a resolution update.
When the incident is resolved, post an explicit resolution with the time it was resolved. Some organizations post a brief post-mortem summary on the status page 24-48 hours later.

runs.text: A status page that shows green while users are experiencing outages is worse than no status page at all. Automate component health checks where possible, and ensure the Comms Lead has authority to post updates without waiting for engineering approval.

The status page tells your customers what is happening. Post early, post often even when there is nothing new to say, and never speculate about root cause. Silence is more alarming than an honest "we are still investigating."

cards.title: Internal vs External Communication
cards.teaser: Internal and external incident communications are different documents for different audiences with different needs. Conflating them — either by making internal communications too vague, or by pasting internal updates to the status page — creates confusion in both directions.

runs.text: Two distinct communication streams run during a significant incident: internal (the war room, engineering Slack, management briefings) and external (the status page, customer emails, social media). The Communications Lead manages both, but the content requirements are fundamentally different.

items.text: Internal communications

can and should include: current best hypothesis, commands being run, systems being checked, specific error messages, names of people assigned to specific tasks, and preliminary root cause theories. The audience needs technical precision to act.
External communications

should include only: what is impacted (which services, which user actions), what is being done (investigating, monitoring, mitigating), and current status (investigating / identified / mitigating / resolved). No technical details, no error codes, no root cause speculation, no blame assignment.

runs.text: Common mistakes in the boundary:

items.text: Posting internal status to the public page.

"We rolled back the 14:05 deployment of service X because it introduced a goroutine leak" is internal information. Customers do not need deployment details; they need to know whether the service is working.
Making internal communications too vague.
"Something is wrong with the API" is not useful in the war room. Engineering needs specifics. Save vagueness for the external channel.
Overpromising in external comms.
"We expect to resolve this within 30 minutes" sets a commitment that the engineering team may not have made. The Comms Lead confirms timelines with the IC before publishing them.

runs.text: PagerDuty's IRP uses a simple heuristic: "Would I be comfortable if this exact sentence were in a TechCrunch article about the outage?" If yes, it is suitable for external communications. If no, it stays internal.

Internal comms are for engineers who need technical precision to act. External comms are for customers who need to know what is broken and whether it is being fixed. Never paste one into the other — they are written for completely different readers.

cards.title: Shift Hand-offs
cards.teaser: An incident that spans a shift boundary is one of the highest-risk moments in incident management. A poor handoff means the incoming team re-investigates what the outgoing team already ruled out, or misses a critical safety constraint on a live system.

runs.text: Multi-hour and multi-day incidents are common in distributed systems. When an incident outlasts a shift, the IC and Ops Lead must hand off to incoming counterparts explicitly. An undisciplined handoff — a quick Slack message saying "it's still broken, good luck" — wastes hours of the incoming team's investigation time.
The handoff checklist (adapted from PagerDuty's IRP):

items.text: Current state summary.
What is the current user impact? Has it improved, worsened, or remained stable since declaration? What is the current severity level?
What has been tried.
List every hypothesis that has been investigated and its outcome. "We ruled out the database at 15:30 because metrics showed normal latency throughout."
Current best theory.
What does the outgoing team believe the root cause is? What evidence supports it?
Active mitigations and risks.
Are there any in-progress changes? Are there any constraints on what can be changed safely? (e.g., "Do not restart the worker fleet — it will drop in-flight payments.")
Next actions.
What is the incoming team expected to do first? What is the priority queue?
Contacts.
Who is available for questions? Who are the relevant subject matter experts who have been involved?

runs.text: The handoff should happen on a live bridge call, not asynchronously. The outgoing IC walks the incoming IC through the document and answers questions. The incoming IC does not take the handoff until they can accurately restate the current state.

Handoffs that happen asynchronously (a written document and no call) routinely miss critical constraints. The incoming team reads the doc, thinks they understand the situation, and then makes a change the outgoing team specifically decided not to make — because the reasoning did not survive the written summary.

A shift handoff during an incident is a formal transfer of knowledge: what is broken, what has been tried, what the current theory is, and what is dangerous to change. It happens on a live call, not in a Slack message, because the outgoing team needs to answer questions, not just write notes.

cards.title: Closing an Incident
cards.teaser: Closing an incident is a formal act — not just "things seem better." The IC declares the incident closed when user impact is resolved, the system is stable, and the immediate risk of recurrence is managed. Not everything gets resolved at close: the post-mortem action items stay open.

runs.text: Incident close is the mirror image of declaration: just as incidents should be declared earlier than most teams are comfortable with, they should be closed as soon as the criteria are met — not held open out of caution or for procedural completeness.
Close criteria (all should be true):

items.text: User impact is resolved.
The affected service is operating within normal SLO parameters. Error rates, latency, and availability are back to baseline.
The system is stable.
Metrics are trending in the right direction and have been stable for a reasonable observation window (typically 15-30 minutes for SEV-1, shorter for lower severities).
Immediate recurrence risk is managed.
Either the root cause has been mitigated, or a compensating control is in place and monitoring is active. "We rolled back the offending deploy and are watching dashboards" is sufficient for close.
The Ops Lead confirms.
The IC gets explicit confirmation from the Ops Lead that there are no outstanding technical risks before declaring close.

runs.text: What stays open after the incident closes:

items.text: The post-mortem.
The post-mortem is scheduled (typically within 72 hours for a SEV-1) but not completed before close. The incident does not stay open waiting for the post-mortem.
Action items.
Permanent fixes, architectural improvements, and monitoring gaps identified during the incident are tracked as action items in the issue tracker — not held open in the incident record.
Monitoring enhancements.
Any gaps in alerting coverage found during the incident are filed as issues and tracked to completion.

runs.text: When the IC declares the incident closed, the Comms Lead posts the final status page update (resolved, with the resolution time), sends the all-clear to internal channels, and updates the incident ticket status. The war room channel is archived, not deleted — it is the permanent record.

Google's IMP includes a formal incident closure review: before declaring closed on a SEV-1, the IC runs through the checklist with the full response team on the bridge. The review takes 5-10 minutes and ensures no one has a concern that would warrant keeping the incident open.

Close the incident when users are no longer impacted and the system is stable. Do not wait for the post-mortem or the permanent fix — those happen after close as tracked action items. Closing is a formal declaration, not a feeling that things seem better.

cards.title: A SEV-1 from Declaration to Close
cards.teaser: Abstract incident theory is useless without a concrete model to match it against. Walking through a real SEV-1 — payment service down, 14:21 UTC — shows how IC, Ops Lead, Comms Lead, and Scribe work together across the full incident lifecycle.

runs.text: Scenario: it is 14:21 UTC on a Tuesday. PagerDuty fires a SEV-1 alert: "payment-service error rate above 50% for 5 minutes." The on-call engineer, Priya, accepts the page.

items.text: 14:21 — Declaration.
Priya checks the alert and confirms 503s on all payment endpoints. She creates a Slack channel
#inc-2024-01-15-payment
, posts: "Declaring SEV-1. Payment service returning 503 for all requests. Need IC and Comms Lead." She pages the incident response rotation.
14:23 — IC and Comms Lead join.
Marcus (IC) and Sasha (Comms Lead) join the channel. Marcus opens the bridge call. Priya becomes Ops Lead. Daniel joins as Scribe and opens the incident timeline document.
14:25 — Status page posted.
Sasha posts to the public status page: "We are investigating an issue affecting payment processing. Updates to follow every 15 minutes."
14:26 — Investigation begins.
Priya (Ops Lead) checks recent deploys. A new build of payment-service was deployed at 14:05. She asks a second engineer to check database connectivity while she reviews the deployment diff.
14:33 — Root cause found.
The 14:05 deployment changed an environment variable name. The service cannot connect to the payment gateway. Rollback is recommended.
14:35 — IC approves rollback.
Marcus: "Approved. Ops Lead, proceed with rollback to v2.13.1." Priya initiates rollback. Scribe notes: "14:35 — Rollback to v2.13.1 initiated by Priya."
14:41 — Service recovering.
Error rates dropping. At 14:45, error rate is below 0.5%, within SLO. Sasha posts: "We have identified and resolved the issue. Services are recovering. We will post a full update shortly."
14:55 — Incident closed.

Marcus runs the closure checklist on the bridge. Priya confirms no outstanding technical risk. Marcus declares the incident closed. Sasha posts the resolution update. Daniel closes the timeline document and files three action items: fix the environment variable naming, add a deployment smoke test for payment gateway connectivity, and improve the alert threshold sensitivity.

runs.text: Total duration: 34 minutes. The roles stayed clean: Marcus never touched the terminal; Priya ran the investigation; Sasha owned all external communications; Daniel built the timeline. The post-mortem is scheduled for Thursday — the incident is closed but the work of preventing recurrence is just beginning.

A 34-minute SEV-1 from alert to close: declare immediately, activate roles in the first two minutes, investigate with dedicated Ops Lead, post the status page within five minutes, make decisions through the IC, and close with a formal checklist. The structure is what made the 34 minutes possible.
